en: So what does /fork do? It's very similar to
/clone. The difference is that /clone simply
copies a session
at the end of the current session, right? So
it just creates a plain copy like that. But
what if you knew that in your session you
wanted to
fork out at an earlier point? For example,
here I got these summaries where I demoed a
feature.
I might not wanna have them in my new
session because they just take up some
context unnecessarily. So instead, I might
want to
fork out at an earlier point. Let's say
before I told it to git commit.
If I wanna do that, I can run
/fork instead of clone,
and that brings up a picker,
a picker where I can navigate to an earlier
turn in this conversation
or to an earlier message I sent to the
client. So that allows me to pick a point
earlier in this conversation
where I want to branch out and clone. And
here I can pick one of my old messages. So
for example, I could pick the git commit one
to make sure that I fork before that message
was sent, before that entire committing and
summarizing stuff here happened. So if I
pick git commit here and hit Enter, now I
forked this and that message, that git
commit message is populated here, but I'll
now not send it. And therefore the session
was cloned at an earlier point.
/fork, you can pick an earlier point if you
know that you don't wanna clone the entire
session. And that's what I did here. So now
I still have that entire feature work in
there, but all the other context is gone.
That is the difference.
If I type /resume, we can now see both
clones and forks here. They look the same,
but we know that we
cloned at different points. With /clone, we
cloned at the end. With
/fork, we cloned at an earlier message.
That is the entire idea here. And now we
could continue with our follow-up message
here.
